title: Digital Media & Flourishing
titleJa: デジタルメディアと成長特論
school: School of Design and Science, Chiba Tech
description: How is digital media shaping our world, our perceptions, and the way we communicate and think? In this course, we explore the mechanisms driving new cultural and societal trends in digital media. We examine the relationship between technology, its functions, and human experience, along with the nature of the digital world and how it influences our lives.
outcomesIntro: I wish the class will guide you to:
outcomes: Develop an understanding of theories of narrative, intergroup contact, digital architecture, and media design.
Explore how concepts such as attention, trust, value, and belonging emerge and operate within digital environments.
Gain hands-on experience creating digital content across formats — writing, visual identity, short-form and long-form video, and AI-assisted design.
Design and critique platform functions, reflecting on how the architecture of digital platforms influences interaction, behaviour, trust, and flourishing.
Consider how digital media shapes encounters across difference, including its potential to both divide and connect people.

schedule.note: Guest speaker: Hiro Kay, NHK World producer

scheduleNotes: Every session meets online on Wednesdays. The November 18 and December 9 classes are three hours long to make up for the class that falls on Silver Week.
This syllabus may change during the semester; any changes will be announced. Revised 19 October 2026.
brandsIntro: In Week 3 each student designed a personal brand from the ground up: a brand guide, a business card, and a story told as a social carousel.
workIntro: Work made in the course by the students, shared with the class of 2026

assignments.title: Group project: one imaginary brand, one platform
assignments.linkText: Group project brief and the three brands
assignments.intro: In the Week 4 breakout each room became a platform and chose one of three imaginary brands. Finish the strategy with your team and present it in class on Wednesday 4 November.

sections.heading: The rooms
sections.text: Each breakout room is a platform. The platform was assigned; the brand was your choice. Tell us who is in your team and which brand you picked in your platform's thread in the Slack channel #digitalmedia-flourishing-2026.

sections.heading: The three brands
sections.text: The briefs are vague on purpose so that you can be creative. The toilet paper can be fancy or cheap and funny; the fisher can be rude or charming. The audience does not have to be in Bhutan or Japan: choose the audience, research what they like, and build the strategy from that.

brands.name: Brand A · Individual · The Fisher
brands.situation: A young person who left the city to become a fisher in the countryside, with no money, trying to make a living as a content creator.
facts: One person, one small boat, very early starts, fish to catch every day, and knows how to cook.
Become a monetisable influencer and make an income from content.
Up to you. City people who dream of leaving? People who cook? Fishing hobbyists? Pick them and research what they watch.

brands.name: Brand B · Team · AI Translation Tool
brands.situation: A software company whose tool gives real-time translation between English, Japanese and Dzongkha. You are the marketer, and you need to promote the company.
facts: A small team with a working app that nobody knows yet.
Get the tool known and used.

Up to you. Exchange students and host families? Tour guides and their guests? Hospitals and clinics? Businesses trading between Japan and Bhutan? Families with one grandparent who speaks one language? Or a market you find yourself.

brands.name: Brand C · Small brand · Toilet Paper
brands.situation: A second-generation family mill with a small staff, making unbleached, slightly organic toilet paper. Nobody knows it yet.
facts: A normal toilet paper from a family mill. Small team, a factory floor, maybe a van.
Get known and increase revenue as soon as possible.
Up to you. It could be fancy or cheap as fuck: flat-sharers, families, cafés and offices buying in bulk, or whoever you decide.

sections.heading: What your strategy needs
sections.text: Build it together in a shared doc. Five parts:

steps.title: How your profile looks on the platform
steps.text: Name, bio, picture, and what the first posts look like together.

steps.title: Your target audience
steps.text: Who you are talking to, and why they are on this platform.

steps.title: The brand image and your competitive strategy
steps.text: What people should feel about the brand, and how it stands apart from everyone else selling the same thing. Look at how similar brands do it.

steps.title: How you will keep the audience engaged
steps.text: Not just reach. How do people come back, follow, save and share? The ladder below shows what the feed rewards.

steps.title: Two or three example posts
steps.text: What they look like, and what you hope people do with them.

sections.heading: The engagement ladder
sections.text: From what is cheap for a stranger to what is expensive, and what the feed rewards. Decide which steps your strategy is aiming for.

image.alt: The engagement ladder: impression, watch time, like, save, share, comment, reply, follow, message
image.caption: Impression, watch time, like, save, share or send, comment, reply, follow, message. Cheap for the stranger on the left; expensive, and what the feed rewards, on the right.

sections.heading: Presenting
sections.text: Each team presents in class on Wednesday 4 November (Week 6). I did not want to constrain the format, so it can be a demo, slides, a presentation, or the example posts themselves. No submission beforehand: you will share your screen and present.
items: Post your team members, your brand and, if you have one, the link to your shared doc in your platform's Slack thread.

assignments.submit: No submission before class. Share your screen and present on Wednesday 4 November. If you want to keep your files somewhere, the Week 4 Drive folder is there for that.

assignments.title: Before class: a reading on how infants learn
assignments.linkText: Reading and questions for this session
assignments.intro: Dr. Gal Raz has set a reading before his session. Note your answers to the two questions before you read, then answer the three questions after.

reading.citation: Raz, G. & Saxe, R. (2020). Learning in Infancy Is Active, Endogenously Motivated, and Depends on the Prefrontal Cortices. Annual Review of Developmental Psychology, 2, 247–268.

skip: The social brain: evidence from adults
The social brain: evidence from infants
before: In their first year of life, would you say humans learn more by A) observing whatever happens to be around them, or B) by actively choosing what to engage with?
What do humans learn first, A) low-level perceptual concepts like color, shapes and movement or B) high-level concepts like social relationships and physical laws (like gravity, collision etc.)?
after: Were you convinced that infants' learning depends on active choice of attentional targets?
Do you agree with the claim that infants have distinct motivations when deciding what to look at?
Which evidence did you find most convincing? Which evidence left some open questions for you?
assignments.submit: Submit your answers before class on Wednesday 28 October.

assignments.title: Premiere Pro guide: edit your Short
assignments.linkText: Premiere Pro guide: edit your Short
assignments.intro: Step by step, from importing your clips to exporting a vertical Short of your morning. The Adobe and Artlist logins are shared in class, not on this page.

blocks.p: By the end of class you export one vertical video of your morning, between 45 seconds and 1 minute 10 seconds long. It must include at least two sound effects and one piece of background music. Do the steps below in order and skip anything marked optional if you run out of time.
Text and color are extras at the end of this guide, for anyone who is ahead or for after class.
Have these five things ready before class begins.

check.title: Premiere installed and opened once.
check.text: Sign in with the Adobe account you were given. SDS students get Adobe Creative Cloud from the IT portal. Bhutan students share one account between two people.

check.title: Your footage.
check.text: 5 to 10 minutes of vertical clips of your morning.

check.title: Headphones.
check.text: You cannot judge sound on laptop speakers.

blocks.p: Shortcuts are written for Mac. On Windows, use Ctrl for Cmd and Alt for Option, unless a step gives a separate Windows key.

sections.heading: Step 1: Put everything in one folder and import

blocks.p: Premiere does not copy your clips into the project. It only remembers where they sit, so put them in their final place first.

steps.title: Make one folder.
steps.text: On your Desktop, create a folder called ex. `MyMorning_YourName`. Inside it, create three folders: `Footage`, `Audio` and `Exports`.

steps.title: Copy your clips from your phone into `Footage`.
Stop moving files.
steps.text: From now on, do not rename or move anything in this folder. If you do, Premiere loses the clip and shows “Media Offline”.
**Open Premiere and click New Project** on the Home screen. You are now in Import mode.

steps.title: Name the project.
steps.text: At the top left, type `MyMorning_YourName` in Project name. In Project location, choose the folder you made in step 1.

steps.title: Select your media.
steps.text: In the middle of the screen, browse to your `Footage` folder and click each clip so it gets a tick. Then open `Audio` and tick your room sound.

steps.title: Turn off Create new sequence.
steps.text: It is in the Import settings on the right. You will make the sequence by hand in Step 3. Leave Copy media off as well.
**Click Create** at the bottom right. Premiere switches to Edit mode and your clips appear in the Project panel, bottom left.
**Save** with Cmd+S. Do this every few minutes for the rest of the class.

blocks.p: To add more files later, press Cmd+I or drag them into the Project panel.

sections.heading: Step 2: Look around the Premiere screen

blocks.p: After you click Create in Step 1, you are looking at this screen. Take two minutes to find each panel before you touch anything.
The screen is a set of panels, and five of them do nearly all the work. The header bar at the top switches between three modes: Import, Edit and Export. You will spend most of your time in Edit.

head: Panel
Where it sits
What it is for
rows: Holds everything you imported: clips, music, images, sequences
Previews a single clip so you can pick the part you want
Where you arrange clips in order; video tracks on top, audio below
Plays back the edit you are building on the timeline
Selection, Razor, Type and the other cursors
Settings for whatever is selected: size, position, text, volume

blocks.p: If a panel disappears, open it again from the Window menu. To put everything back, choose Window > Workspaces > Reset to Saved Layout. Press the backtick key (`) with the mouse over any panel to make it full screen, and again to shrink it.

sections.heading: Step 3: Create the sequence for a Short

blocks.p: A sequence is one timeline. Today you set it up by hand so it is vertical, 30 frames per second, and in normal color.

steps.text: **Choose File > New > Sequence**, or press Cmd+N.
**Click the Settings tab** at the top of the New Sequence window.

steps.title: Editing Mode:
steps.text: choose Custom.

steps.title: Timebase:
steps.text: choose “Social Media Portrait 9x16 30fps”
sub: Frame size: type 1080 for horizontal and 1920 for vertical.
**Working Color Space:** Rec. 709. This stops iPhone HDR clips from looking too bright or grey.

steps.title: Sequence Name:
steps.text: type ex.`My Morning` at the bottom and click OK. An empty timeline opens, and the Program Monitor at the top right shows a tall black frame.

steps.title: Test with one clip.
steps.text: Drag any clip from the Project panel onto track V1 of the timeline. If a Clip Mismatch Warning appears, choose Keep existing settings (IMPORTANT!).

steps.title: Look at the picture in the Program Monitor.
steps.text: Fix it now if something is wrong:
sub: **The clip looks zoomed in.** It was filmed in 4K. Right-click the clip on the timeline and choose Set to Frame Size.
**The clip is landscape with black bars.** Select it, open the Properties panel on the right, and raise Scale until it fills the frame. Then change Position to choose which part you see.

**The clip looks too bright or washed out.** It is HDR. In the Project panel, select all clips with Cmd+A, right-click, and choose Modify > Interpret Footage. Under Color Management, set the color space override to Rec. 709 and click OK. If you cannot find this setting, call Daum before you go on.

steps.text: **Delete the test clip** from the timeline and save.

blocks.p: Your Short should be between 45 seconds and 1 minute 10 seconds.

list.title: Why not shorter.
list.text: Under 45 seconds there is not enough room for a beginning, a middle and an end.

list.title: Why not longer.
list.text: YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels allow up to 3 minutes, but people swipe away fast. Platforms show a video to more people when viewers watch it to the end.

list.title: The first second.
list.text: Put your strongest image first. Do not start with a title or a slow shot.

list.title: Vertical and full screen.
list.text: Keep anything important away from the very top and bottom, where the app puts its own buttons and text.

blocks.p: You edit in two passes. First a rough cut, then you tighten it.
Get your best shots onto the timeline in order. Aim for about 90-120 seconds and do not polish anything yet.

steps.title: Open a clip.
steps.text: Double-click it in the Project panel. It appears in the Source Monitor, top left.

steps.title: Watch it.
steps.text: Press Space to play and pause. L plays forward, J plays backward, K stops. Tap L twice to go faster.

steps.title: Mark the good part.
steps.text: Press I where the useful part starts and O where it ends. Keep each piece short, about 2 to 5 seconds.

steps.title: Add it to the timeline.
steps.text: Drag the picture from the Source Monitor onto track V1, right after the previous clip. It snaps into place. The comma key (,) does the same at the playhead.

steps.title: Repeat for every shot you want.
steps.text: Use the same action in different sizes: wide, then medium, then close-up.

steps.title: Choose your first shot.
steps.text: Put your strongest image first. A viewer decides in the first second whether to keep watching.

steps.title: Play the whole thing.
steps.text: Click at the start of the timeline and press Space.

steps.title: Check the length.
steps.text: The timecode at the bottom right of the Program Monitor shows the total. Stop adding clips at about 90 seconds.

blocks.p: Two things confuse most beginners. The blue buttons at the left of each track (V1, A1) decide where new clips land, so keep V1 and A1 blue. The magnet icon (snapping, S) makes clips click together edge to edge, so leave it on.
Now remove everything the video does not need. Most of the work is making each clip shorter.

steps.title: Trim an edge.
steps.text: With the Selection tool (V), move the mouse to the edge of a clip until a red bracket appears, then drag.

steps.title: Trim faster with Q and W.
steps.text: Put the playhead where the clip should start and press Q. Put it where the clip should end and press W. Premiere closes the gap for you.

steps.title: Cut out the middle of a clip.
steps.text: Put the playhead at the start of the bad part and press Cmd+K. Do the same at its end. Click the bad piece and press Option+Delete. On Windows, press Shift+Delete. The clips after it slide left.

steps.title: Close a gap.
steps.text: Click the empty space between two clips and press Delete.

steps.title: Change the order.
steps.text: Hold Cmd+Option and drag a clip between two others. On Windows, hold Ctrl+Alt. The clip moves and nothing is overwritten.

steps.title: Build a rhythm.
steps.text: Try several very short clips of half a second to one second, then one long shot of 4 to 5 seconds. The contrast is what makes it feel edited.

steps.title: Check the length again.
steps.text: Stop when the total is between 45 seconds and 1 minute 10 seconds.

blocks.p: Viewers forgive rough pictures sooner than rough sound. Put your headphones on now and keep them on until you export.

steps.text: **Go to artlist.io** and click Sign in.

steps.title: Sign in with the class account.
steps.text: Daum gives you the email and password in class. Please do not change the password or any account setting.

steps.title: Find your music.
steps.text: Click Music. Type the one word for your morning in the search bar, for example cozy, calm or funny. You can also filter by mood, genre and instrument. Choose a track without vocals.

steps.title: Listen before you download.
steps.text: Press play and imagine your first ten seconds. Does it fit?

steps.title: Download it.
steps.text: Click the download arrow next to the track. Choose WAV, or MP3 if your internet is slow.

steps.title: Find two sound effects.
steps.text: Click SFX and search for what you need: whoosh, pop, door, alarm, footsteps. Download each one.

steps.title: Move the files into your `Audio` folder.
steps.text: They arrive in your Downloads folder. Move them now, before you import them.

steps.title: Import them.
steps.text: In Premiere press Cmd+I, select the new files in your `Audio` folder, and click Import.

blocks.p: Artlist is a paid licence, so you do not need to credit its music. If you use a sound from Freesound or another Creative Commons site, write the title, author, source and licence in your caption.
Export one H.264 .mp4 file at 1080×1920. Start this step by 2 hours 30 minutes into class.

steps.text: **Click anywhere on the timeline** so the panel has a blue outline. Premiere exports whichever panel is active.

steps.title: Open Export.
steps.text: Press Cmd+M, or click Export in the header bar at the top.

steps.title: File name:
steps.text: type `MyMorning_YourName`.

steps.title: Location:
steps.text: click it and choose your `Exports` folder.

steps.title: Preset:
steps.text: choose Match Source – Adaptive High Bitrate. Format should read H.264.

steps.title: Check the Video section.
steps.text: Frame size must read 1080×1920 and frame rate 30. If it shows 1920×1080, your sequence is not vertical, so go back to Step 3.

steps.title: Check the Range.
steps.text: It should say Entire Source. The preview on the right should show your whole video, between 45 seconds and 1 minute 10.
**Click Export** at the bottom right and wait for the bar to finish.

steps.title: Watch the file.
steps.text: Open the .mp4 from your `Exports` folder and watch it from start to end, with sound. Send it to your phone and watch it there too.
Drop your final file [📁 here.](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1DNiMXkCvhHSnok7IKS02oMi1hj9p-E9e?usp=sharing)

blocks.p: For other kinds of video later, use these settings.

head: Destination
Frame size
Format and preset
rows: H.264, Match Source – Adaptive High Bitrate
H.264, Match Source – Adaptive High Bitrate
H.264, Match Source – Adaptive Medium Bitrate
Hand-off to another editor or broadcaster

blocks.p: Only do this step if your cut and your sound are finished. One line of text is enough for a short video.

steps.title: Go to the place where the text should appear.
steps.text: Move the playhead there.
**Pick the Type tool** by pressing T. Click on the picture in the Program Monitor and type.
**Switch back to the Selection tool** by pressing V. Otherwise every click makes a new text box.

steps.title: Style it.
steps.text: With the text selected, use the Properties panel on the right to change font, size and color. Use the align buttons there to center it.

steps.title: Keep it in the middle of the frame.
steps.text: The top and bottom of a vertical video are covered by the app’s own buttons and captions.

steps.title: Set how long it stays.
steps.text: The text is its own clip on track V2. Drag its edges on the timeline.

steps.title: Captions, only if you speak in the video.
steps.text: Open Window > Text, go to the Transcript tab and transcribe the sequence. Then click Create Captions and read them through once.

steps.title: Transitions.
steps.text: A plain cut is right most of the time. For a soft change, click a cut and press Cmd+D to add a cross dissolve.

blocks.p: Basic correction means making each shot look natural and making the shots match each other.

steps.title: Open the panel.
steps.text: Choose Window > Lumetri Color and stay in the Basic Correction section.
**Select one clip** on the timeline.

steps.title: Try Auto first.
steps.text: Click the Auto button. If it looks worse, press Cmd+Z.

steps.title: White balance.
steps.text: Click the eyedropper on something that should be white or grey, or move Temperature until skin looks right.

steps.title: Exposure and contrast.
steps.text: Brighten or darken with Exposure, then add a little Contrast.

steps.title: Highlights and shadows.
steps.text: Pull Highlights down if a window is blown out. Lift Shadows if a face is too dark.

steps.title: Saturation.
steps.text: Small moves only. Around 100 to 115 is usually enough.

steps.title: Make it feel like morning.
steps.text: Move Temperature a little toward orange and raise Exposure slightly. This helps if you filmed later in the day.

steps.title: Repeat for the clips that look different from the rest.

blocks.p: To give the whole video one look, choose New Item > Adjustment Layer in the Project panel, lay it on a track above your clips, and apply Lumetri to that layer instead of to each clip.
These sixteen cover most of a first edit. Learn J, K, L and the trimming keys first; they save the most time.

head: Action
Shortcut
rows: Play backward / stop / play forward (tap again to speed up)
Trim start / end of clip to playhead

sections.heading: Good habits and what to learn next

blocks.p: Most beginner trouble comes from four things, and each has a simple fix.

list.title: “Media Offline” in red.
list.text: You moved or renamed a file after importing. Right-click the clip > Link Media and point Premiere to the new location. Avoid it by not moving files once a project has started.

list.title: Lost work.
list.text: Press Cmd+S often. Auto-save is on by default, and backups sit in the Adobe Premiere Auto-Save folder next to your project file.

list.title: Choppy playback.
list.text: Lower the playback resolution in the Program Monitor from Full to 1/2 or 1/4. This changes the preview only, not the export.

list.title: Polishing too early.
list.text: Finish the rough order of the whole video before you touch color, titles or effects.

blocks.p: Once a full edit feels comfortable, the next skills worth adding are keyframes (animating position, scale or volume over time), multi-camera editing for interviews, and the newer AI tools such as Object Mask and Generative Extend. Adobe lists what each release added on its [what’s new page](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere-pro/using/whats-new.html).

list.text: [Adobe Premiere desktop release notes](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/whats-new/release-notes.html): current version and system requirements
[PetaPixel, 20 January 2026](https://petapixel.com/2026/01/20/rebranded-adobe-premiere-26-arrives-with-one-click-object-tracking): the rename to Adobe Premiere and Object Mask
[Adobe: import media into a new project](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere-pro-next/organize-media/import-files/import-media-into-a-new-project.html): Import mode and the Create new sequence switch

blocks.p: The editing steps and shortcuts are standard Premiere defaults, written from general knowledge of the app rather than taken from these pages.

assignments.submit: Export your Short as one .mp4 file named MyMorning_YourName and drop it in the Week 8 Drive folder.

assignments.title: Final Project: A Brand for Life
assignments.linkText: Final project brief: A Brand for Life
assignments.intro: In a team of three to five, create a brand that brings awareness to the theme of life. Teams present on Wednesday 16 December (Week 12).

blocks.p: The world is polarised right now, and social media shows it every day. Everyone seems very sure about how to live, what is right, and who is wrong. Ask most people directly, though, and they do not really know.

So this project goes back to a fundamental question. What is the value of a life? What does it mean to live, and why do people live? In Week 1 we explored three answers to what makes a life go well: pleasure, getting what you want, and a list of things that are good for anyone.

Now think of yourself as a social media content creator. You write, you film, you post, you generate, you share your thoughts with the world. What is it for? Is it to feel satisfied? Is it for the world to hear you and become a little better? Or is it to bring in attention?

Attention is not a bad thing in itself, but it is not a small thing either. When someone watches a video for one minute, they give one minute of their life, and they do not get it back. Social media has metrics to count those minutes and to maximise them. Look at all the junk that has been created for those numbers: videos nobody needed, posts made only to be counted, the same thing copied a thousand times. Every one of them took a minute from somebody. With AI, junk can now be made faster than anyone can watch it.
But at the end it is a tool, and it is up to the person holding it to decide. Unlike most tools, though, the feed asks to be picked up. That makes deciding harder, and it makes it matter more.

You now know the tools that are given to you: writing, brand identity, platforms, attention, video and sound. So here is the project. What kind of brand can you design on the theme of life? Before you make one more thing, ask whether the world needs this one.

Your brand can be about artificial life, life in a digital space, or the life of a person. Take advantage of what social media does well, such as reach, format, community, and the pull of a short film, and use it to do good for people. The same mechanics that spread junk can carry something worth a minute of someone's life.

Your brand needs to answer one question: how does a person feel and live after spending time with it? State what flourishing means for your audience, whether that is connection, understanding, rest, courage, a lingering memory, or something else. Show how the brand, the account, the video and the community design all serve it. Say too how you would know people are better off, because views and likes will not tell you.

sections.heading: Choose one category
sections.text: Each category is a different way in. These are only sparks. Go somewhere we haven't thought of.

steps.title: Influencer
steps.text: It could be an individual. A life that people follow. A person, an animal, a tree, a city, a future version of you.

steps.title: Product brand
steps.text: Something people can hold, use or buy that carries the idea. An object, a tool, an app, a ritual in a box, software.

steps.title: Movement
steps.text: An invitation to live differently, even for one day. Quiet or loud, tiny or global.

steps.title: Community
steps.text: A place people fill with their own lives. Online, offline, or both.

steps.title: Education institute
steps.text: Something that teaches or guides us towards the message you want to share about life.

steps.title: Brand deck
steps.text: Who it is for, what it stands for, name, visual identity and voice. It should include a community strategy: how you keep people engaged after the launch post, and how it helps their lives.

steps.title: A real social media account
steps.text: On one platform, with at least five posts, and a clear argument for why that platform and not another.

steps.title: A three-minute video that introduces the brand
A team sheet
steps.text: Who is producer, director, editor, community manager, designer (or other roles you define), and what each person made.

assignments.submit: Each team presents its final project in class on Wednesday 16 December (Week 12).
